subject: Follow-up: end-to-end latency checks (p95/p99) — prefetch & streaming clarifications
messages:
From: Alex Wong <alex.wong@orionhealth.ai>
To: hiro_tanaka@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: 2026-02-17T15:12:00Z
Subject: Post-call: our current p95/p99 numbers + streaming gotchas

Thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap from our side so we have a clear baseline for the performance qualification:

- Current provider: p95 (end-to-end) ≈ 730 ms, p99 ≈ 1.6 s (measured on production traffic; includes network & client serialization).
- Typical request: ~64 tokens average, single-choice completions via streaming.
- Concurrency: normal 20–30, burst up to ~80 sustained for 5–10 minutes during peak windows.
- Concern: partial-streaming behaviour (client displays incremental chunks) seems to add tail variance; cold workers add additional ~400–700ms on first few requests after idle.

I've attached a small CSV with an anonymized latency snapshot and a short log segment showing two cold-start spikes. Can Redwood confirm whether your hosted offering (streaming enabled) can meet p95 ≤ 250 ms and p99 ≤ 700 ms for our typical short requests, or should we expect different targets? Also curious how you measure p99 (server-side vs full e2e).

Next steps from our side: Priya can share a sanitized trace of a 60-second peak window if that helps. Would also like to see a concrete run plan for a hosted test.

Thanks,
Alex Wong
Head of Platform — Orion HealthAI
Attachments: orion_latency_snapshot_20260217.csv (csv), verbose_logs_segment.txt (txt)

From: hiro_tanaka@redwood.com
To: Alex Wong <alex.wong@orionhealth.ai>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.com, ben_carter@redwood.com
Date: 2026-02-17T17:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call: our current p95/p99 numbers + streaming gotchas

Alex — thanks for sending this over and for the clear numbers. Short answers up front: we can often hit p95 in the low hundreds for short, streaming-enabled completions on our hosted API, but the p99 depends heavily on burst concurrency, client-side measurement boundaries, and whether your p99 window includes cold-worker startup.

A few clarifying asks so our test plan is aligned:
- When you report p95/p99 above, is that: (A) measured at your client (full e2e including client-app glue/serialization) or (B) measured at an intermediate edge (our provider's edge -> model runtime)? Please state where timestamps start/stop.
- Are the averages you sent (64 tokens) including prompt + generation tokens or generation-only?
- During bursts (up to ~80), do requests arrive as a uniform steady stream or as concentrated spikes (e.g., 80 concurrent at T0)?
- Do you rely on long-lived KV/cache warming between requests, or are most requests to cold contexts?

Proposed initial acceptance thresholds (hosted test baseline) we can aim for in a 48-hour run with traffic shaping that mirrors your peaks:
- p95 (end-to-end, server measured to final token emitted): <= 220 ms for single-turn short completions (~60 tokens)
- p99 (same measurement): <= 620 ms

These targets assume: streaming enabled, no large batching (N=1 typical), concurrency shaped to your burst profile, and warm runtime pool (we'll keep workers warm during the test). If your p99 measurement includes client rendering time we should add a realistic client overhead margin (~100–300 ms).

If you can confirm the measurement origin and share the 60s peak trace, we'll produce a short-hosted run plan (traffic shaping script + config: concurrency, keepalive, KV prefetch, streaming chunk size) and a pass/fail checklist.

I'll loop Ben (SRE/bench lead) and Marissa (account lead) to draft the plan once we get the trace.

— Hiro Tanaka
SRE, Performance Qualification — Redwood Inference

From: Priya Sharma <priya@orionhealth.ai>
To: hiro_tanaka@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Cc: Alex Wong <alex.wong@orionhealth.ai>
Date: 2026-02-18T09:30:00Z
Subject: Re: Post-call: our current p95/p99 numbers + streaming gotchas

Thanks, Hiro — good questions. Responses below and attached sanitized traces/logs.

- Measurement origin: our SREs measure at the client SDK layer (full e2e, includes mobile/web rendering time). The CSV you received has the client-side timestamps.
- Token accounting: 64 tokens is average total (prompt + generated). Typical prompt size ~20–30 tokens; generated ~34–44 tokens.
- Burst profile: it's usually a concentrated spike — many requests arrive within a 10–20 second window, not evenly spread. We can reconstruct a 60s peak window to simulate.
- Cache/warmth: we see some requests hit warmed contexts (repeat dialogs), but a fair percentage are effectively cold — first request after 5+ min idle shows the cold-worker penalty.

Attachments included: sanitized_peak_60s_trace.json, cold_start_samples.txt (we've redacted PII).

One follow-up: how does Redwood handle streaming chunking and client flush behavior? Our front-end relies on small chunks so the user perceives typing. If chunking causes head-of-line blocking or larger latency per-emit, we may lose perceived responsiveness.

Happy to share the 60s trace — let us know desired format.

— Priya
Principal SRE — Orion HealthAI

On 2026-02-17 at 17:03, hiro_tanaka@redwood.com wrote:
> Alex — thanks for sending this over and for the clear numbers...

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Priya Sharma <priya@orionhealth.ai>, Alex Wong <alex.wong@orionhealth.ai>
Cc: hiro_tanaka@redwood.com, marissa_cole@redwood.com
Date: 2026-02-19T09:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Follow-up: end-to-end latency checks (p95/p99) — prefetch & streaming clarifications

Hi Priya / Alex — thanks for the extra details and the traces. We read the client-side logs; very helpful. Couple concrete notes and a proposed next step:

Summary observations from the traces:
- The client-side p95/p99 maps closely to server-side but adds a variable render/serialize overhead (~120–280 ms).
- Cold-worker spikes in the logs align with provisioning events and kernel JIT times (~350–650 ms extra).
- The concentrated spike profile (80 concurrent in 10–20s) is the core tail driver.

Proposed hosted qualification run (48h controlled):
- Scope: mirror your 60s peak as a repeating waveform over 48h with 6–8 peaks/hour (configurable).
- Target config: streaming ON, streaming_chunk_bytes ~512, max_concurrency_override = 80, batching disabled (N=1), kv_prefetch_on_request = true (TTL 120s).
- Measurement method: we will measure server-side end-to-end (time from API receive to final token sent), and we will also provide a combined view that adds your client-side average render delta so you can compare numbers apples-to-apples.
- Pass criteria (server-side): p95 ≤ 220 ms, p99 ≤ 620 ms for the representative short requests. For your client-measured p99 target, allow for the client delta we observed.

Actions we need from Orion:
1) Confirm you will provide the 60s peak trace in JSON (ideally the sanitized_peak_60s_trace.json you mentioned).
2) Provide a sandbox API key or authorize sandbox traffic from a test IP range so we can run the shaped load.
3) Optional: provide a short sample of the front-end rendering pipeline (one example) so we can include the client-serialize step in combined metrics.

I'll attach a short run-plan doc (plan_hosted_run_Orion.pdf) and a traffic-shaping script stub; once we have the trace and key, we propose starting the run next Tuesday (2026-02-24) and delivering a 48h report within 72 hours of completion.

If that schedule works we'll loop in our infra to reserve warm pools and set the keepalive policy to avoid cold-worker gaps.

Best,
Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference
Attachments: plan_hosted_run_Orion.pdf (pdf), traffic_shaping_stub.sh (sh)
